{{Short description|Stochastic model for the evolution of financial interest rates}}
[[Image:SQRTDiffusion.png|thumb|Three trajectories of CIR processes]]
In [[mathematical finance]], the '''Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) model''' describes the evolution of [[interest rate]]s. It is a type of "one factor model" ([[short-rate model]]) as it describes interest rate movements as driven by only one source of [[market risk]]. The model can be used in the valuation of [[interest rate derivative]]s. It was introduced in 1985<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Theory of the Term Structure of Interest Rates - The Econometric Society |url=http://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/econometrica/1985/03/01/theory-term-structure-interest-rates |access-date=2023-10-14 |website=www.econometricsociety.org |language=en}}</ref> by [[John C. Cox]], [[Jonathan E. Ingersoll]] and [[Stephen Ross (economist)|Stephen A. Ross]] as an extension of the [[Vasicek model]], itself an [[Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process]].

== The model ==
[[File:CIR Process.png|thumb|right|CIR process]]
The CIR model describes the instantaneous interest rate <math>r_t</math> with a [[William Feller|Feller]] square-root process, whose [[stochastic differential equation]] is

:<math>dr_t = a(b-r_t)\, dt + \sigma\sqrt{r_t}\, dW_t,</math>

where <math>W_t</math> is a [[Wiener process]] (modelling the random market risk factor) and <math> a </math>, <math> b </math>, and <math> \sigma\, </math> are the [[parameter]]s. The parameter <math> a </math> corresponds to the speed of adjustment to the mean <math> b </math>, and <math> \sigma\, </math> to volatility. The drift factor, <math> a(b-r_t)</math>, is exactly the same as in the Vasicek model. It ensures [[mean reversion (finance)|mean reversion]] of the interest rate towards the long run value <math>b</math>, with speed of adjustment governed by the strictly positive parameter <math>a</math>.

The [[standard deviation]] factor, <math>\sigma \sqrt{r_t}</math>, avoids the possibility of negative interest rates for all positive values of <math>a</math> and <math>b</math>.
An interest rate of zero is also precluded if the condition

:<math>2 a b \geq \sigma^2 \,</math>

is met. More generally, when the rate (<math>r_t</math>) is close to zero, the standard deviation (<math>\sigma \sqrt{r_t}</math>) also becomes very small, which dampens the effect of the random shock on the rate. Consequently, when the rate gets close to zero, its evolution becomes dominated by the drift factor, which pushes the rate upwards (towards [[steady state|equilibrium]]).

In the case <math>4 a b =\sigma^2 \,</math>,<ref>Yuliya Mishura, Andrey Pilipenko & Anton Yurchenko-Tytarenko(10 Jan 2024): Low-dimensional Cox-Ingersoll-Ross process, Stochastics, DOI:10.1080/17442508.2023.2300291</ref> the Feller square-root process can be obtained from the square of an [[Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process]]. It is [[ergodic]] and possesses a stationary distribution. It is used in the [[Heston model]] to model stochastic volatility.

===Distribution===
* Future distribution
: The distribution of future values of a CIR process can be computed in closed form:
:: <math>r_{t+T} = \frac{Y}{2c},</math>
: where <math>c=\frac{2a}{(1 - e^{-aT})\sigma^2}</math>, and ''Y'' is a [[noncentral chi-squared distribution|non-central chi-squared distribution]] with <math>\frac{4ab}{\sigma^2}</math> degrees of freedom and non-centrality parameter <math>2 c r_te^{-aT}</math>. Formally the probability density function is:

:: <math>f(r_{t+T};r_t,a,b,\sigma)=c\,e^{-u-v} \left (\frac{v}{u}\right)^{q/2} I_{q}(2\sqrt{uv}), </math>

: where <math>q = \frac{2ab}{\sigma^2}-1</math>, <math>u = c r_t e^{-aT}</math>, <math>v = c r_{t+T}</math>, and <math>I_{q}(2\sqrt{uv})</math> is a modified Bessel function of the first kind of order <math>q</math>.
* Asymptotic distribution
: Due to mean reversion, as time becomes large, the distribution of <math>r_{\infty}</math> will approach a [[gamma distribution]] with the probability density of:
:: <math>f(r_\infty;a,b,\sigma)=\frac{\beta^\alpha}{\Gamma(\alpha)}r_\infty^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta r_\infty},</math>
: where <math>\beta = 2a/\sigma^2 </math> and <math> \alpha = 2ab/\sigma^2 </math>.
{{Collapse top|title=Derivation of asymptotic distribution}}
To derive the asymptotic distribution <math>p_{\infty}</math> for the CIR model, we must use the [[Fokker–Planck equation]]:

:<math>{\partial p\over{\partial t}} + {\partial\over{\partial r}}[a(b-r)p] = {1\over{2}}\sigma^{2}{\partial^{2}\over{\partial r^{2}}}(rp)</math>

Our interest is in the particular case when <math>\partial_{t}p \rightarrow 0</math>, which leads to the simplified equation:

:<math>a(b-r)p_{\infty} = {1\over{2}}\sigma^{2}\left(p_{\infty} + r{dp_{\infty}\over{dr}} \right)</math>

Defining <math>\alpha = 2ab/\sigma^{2}</math> and <math>\beta = 2a/\sigma^{2}</math> and rearranging terms leads to the equation:

:<math>{\alpha-1\over{r}} - \beta = {d\over{dr}} \log p_{\infty}</math>

Integrating shows us that:

:<math>p_{\infty} \propto r^{\alpha-1}e^{-\beta r}</math>

Over the range <math>p_{\infty} \in (0,\infty]</math>, this density describes a gamma distribution. Therefore, the asymptotic distribution of the CIR model is a gamma distribution.
{{Collapse bottom}}

===Properties===
* [[Mean reversion (finance)|Mean reversion]],
* Level dependent volatility (<math>\sigma \sqrt{r_t}</math>),
* For given positive <math>r_0</math> the process will never touch zero, if <math>2 a b \geq\sigma^2</math>; otherwise it can occasionally touch the zero point,
* <math>\operatorname E[r_t\mid r_0]=r_0 e^{-at} + b (1-e^{-at})</math>, so long term mean is <math>b</math>,
* <math>\operatorname{Var}[r_t\mid r_0]=r_0 \frac{\sigma^2}{a} (e^{- a t}-e^{-2a t}) + \frac{b \sigma^2}{2 a}(1-e^{- a t})^2.</math>

===Calibration===
* [[Ordinary least squares]]
: The continuous SDE can be discretized as follows

:: <math> r_{t+\Delta t}-r_t = a (b-r_t)\,\Delta t + \sigma\, \sqrt{r_t \Delta t} \varepsilon_t, </math>

:which is equivalent to

:: <math> \frac{r_{t+\Delta t}-r_t}{\sqrt r_t} =\frac{ab\Delta t}{\sqrt r_t}-a \sqrt r_t\Delta t + \sigma\, \sqrt{\Delta t} \varepsilon_t, </math>
:provided <math>\varepsilon_t</math> is n.i.i.d. (0,1). This equation can be used for a linear regression.
* Martingale estimation
* [[Maximum likelihood estimation]]

===Simulation===
[[Stochastic simulation]] of the CIR process can be achieved using two variants:
* [[Discretization]]
* Exact

==Bond pricing==
Under the [[No-arbitrage bounds|no-arbitrage assumption]], a bond may be priced using this interest rate process. The bond price is exponential affine in the interest rate:

:<math>P(t,T) = A(t,T) e^{-B(t,T) r_t}\!</math>

where

:<math>A(t,T) = \left(\frac{2h e^{(a+h)(T-t)/2}}{2h + (a+h)(e^{h(T-t)} -1)}\right)^{2ab/\sigma^2}</math>

:<math>B(t,T) = \frac{2(e^{h(T-t)}-1)}{2h+(a+h)(e^{h(T-t)}-1)}</math>

:<math>h = \sqrt{a^2+2\sigma^2}</math>

==Extensions==
The CIR model uses a special case of a [[basic affine jump diffusion]], which still permits a [[closed-form expression]] for bond prices. Time varying functions replacing coefficients can be introduced in the model in order to make it consistent with a pre-assigned term structure of interest rates and possibly volatilities. The most general approach is in Maghsoodi (1996).<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Maghsoodi |first=Yoosef |date=January 1996 |title=Solution of the Extended Cir Term Structure and Bond Option Valuation |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1467-9965.1996.tb00113.x |journal=Mathematical Finance |language=en |volume=6 |issue=1 |pages=89–109 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9965.1996.tb00113.x |issn=0960-1627|url-access=subscription }}</ref> A more tractable approach is in Brigo and Mercurio (2001b)<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brigo |first1=Damiano |last2=Mercurio |first2=Fabio |date=2001-07-01 |title=A deterministic–shift extension of analytically–tractable and time–homogeneous short–rate models |url=https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00013541 |journal=Finance and Stochastics |language=en |volume=5 |issue=3 |pages=369–387 |doi=10.1007/PL00013541 |s2cid=35316609 |issn=0949-2984|url-access=subscription }}</ref> where an external time-dependent shift is added to the model for consistency with an input term structure of rates.

A significant extension of the CIR model to the case of stochastic mean and [[stochastic volatility]] is given by [[Chen model|Lin Chen]] (1996) and is known as [[Chen model]]. A more recent extension for handling cluster volatility, negative interest rates and different distributions is the so-called "CIR #" by Orlando, Mininni and Bufalo (2018,<ref>{{cite book
